sentences.text: Orthacanthus was an extinct genus of freshwater cartilaginous fish belonging to the order Xenacanthiformes, a group of shark-like fish.
Mature individuals of this species could reach a length of nearly 3 meters.
Their teeth possessed at least three cusps, including two principal serrated cusps and an intermediate cusp with complex base morphology.
The larger teeth of O. compressus are distinguished from those of O. texensis by a more pronounced basal tubercle.
Juvenile O. compressus teeth were longer than wide, had thin bases, and lacked serrations.

Dorsal spines of O. platypternus preserve a highly vascularized wall composed mainly of centrifugally growing dentine that grows from a deep dermal position forming trabecular dentine to a superficial location forming lamellar dentine.
Evidence suggests that adult Orthacanthus practiced filial cannibalism by preying on juveniles of their own species when food was scarce.
Triodus spines found inside the mouth cavity of Orthacanthus fossils provide direct evidence of predation.
Orthacanthus produced spiral-shaped feces because of its corkscrew-shaped rectum.
The genus Orthacanthus was named by Louis Agassiz in 1843.
Louis Agassiz erected the genera Orthacanthus and Pleuracanthus based on isolated ichthyodorulites found in the British Carboniferous System.
The initial fossils of Orthacanthus were found in the United Kingdom at locations including Dudley, Leeds, North Wales, Carluke, and Edinburgh.
A well-preserved impression of Orthacanthus from Ruppelsdorf, Bohemia, was described by Goldfuss.
The genus Orthacanthus contains three species: O. arcuatus, O. cylindricus, and O. senckenbergianus.
Orthacanthus lived a nektobenthic lifestyle and had a carnivorous diet.
Isotopic analysis suggests that O. buxieri inhabited freshwater lakes.
Researchers suggest that the size difference between large and small adult teeth in O. compressus might indicate sexual dimorphism.
Analysis of O. platypternus spines indicates sexual dimorphism, with females possessing larger spines than males in subadult and young adult stages.
The periodic deposition of dentine layers in O. platypternus spines likely corresponds to seasonal changes in water temperature and food availability.
The type species for the genus Orthacanthus is Pleuracanthus cylindricus.
Orthacanthus lived during the Upper Carboniferous to the Lower Permian periods.
The oldest known Orthacanthus fossil dates to the Lower Devonian, approximately 407 to 393 million years ago.
Orthacanthus fossils have been discovered in the US, UK, Poland, and France.
About 260 million years ago, Orthacanthus was a top predator in freshwater swamps and bayous across Europe and North America.
There is an ongoing scientific debate regarding whether Orthacanthus had an obligate freshwater lifestyle or a euryhaline diadromous one.
